A bramble is a wild, prickly plant — specifically, a shrub with tough, thorny or spiny stems that tends to grow in a wild, tangled, spreading way. Think of the kind of rough, scratchy bush you might find growing along a countryside fence, at the edge of a forest, or taking over an abandoned garden. That's a bramble.

The word most often refers to plants from a group called Rubus — a large family of plants that includes blackberry bushes and raspberry bushes. In everyday use, especially in British English, "bramble" most commonly means the wild blackberry plant specifically.

Picture a shrub with long, arching, woody stems covered in sharp thorns or prickles (much like a rose bush). These stems, called canes, can be quite long — sometimes several feet — and they arc outward and droop toward the ground. The leaves are usually serrated (jagged-edged), and the plant produces small white or pink flowers in summer, which then develop into the familiar dark, clustered berries.

A key feature of brambles is that they spread aggressively. When a long cane bends down and its tip touches the soil, it can take root there and start a new plant. This is why brambles often form large, dense, impenetrable thickets.

In British English especially, the word "bramble" is also used to refer to the berry itself — i.e., the blackberry. So a British person might say "I went picking brambles" and they mean they were harvesting wild blackberries. You'll also see products like bramble jam or bramble pie, which are simply blackberry jam and blackberry pie.

The word is very commonly used in the plural — "brambles" — to describe a mass or tangle of these prickly plants growing together. A "patch of brambles" or a "bramble thicket" refers to that dense, scratchy, hard-to-walk-through cluster of wild thorny shrubs you might encounter in the wild. Trying to push through it would leave you scratched and snagged.

Because brambles are tangled, sharp, and difficult to get through, the word is sometimes used figuratively in writing or speech to describe anything that is complicated, messy, or full of obstacles. For example: "The new law is a bramble of contradictions" — meaning it's a complicated, thorny mess. This usage is less common in everyday conversation but you'll encounter it in literature.

• "The old garden had been taken over by brambles, and you couldn't walk two steps without getting scratched."
  • "We found a gap in the hedge and crawled through, careful to avoid the bramble stems."
  • "She came back from her walk with scratches on her arms from the brambles along the trail."
  • "The children went out in autumn to pick brambles from the hedgerows." (British usage — picking wild blackberries)
  • "A fox had made its den deep in the bramble thicket, hidden from view."

A bramble is a wild, thorny shrub — most commonly the blackberry or raspberry plant — known for its prickly, arching stems and its tendency to grow in dense, tangled, hard-to-penetrate thickets, and in British English, the word can also refer to the blackberry fruit that the plant produces.
